full_text:
Immortal Aphrodite of the shimmering throne,
child of Zeus, weaver of wiles, I beg you,
do not break my spirit, lady, with anguish
and pain,
but come here, if ever before, at another time,
you heard my voice from far off
and listened, and leaving your father's house
you came, golden,
having yoked your chariot. Beautiful swift sparrows
brought you above the black earth,
whirring their wings fast and thick, down from heaven through the middle air.
Swiftly they arrived; and you, blessed one,
smiling with your immortal face,
asked what I had suffered this time, and why
I was calling you again,
and what, in my maddened heart,
I most wanted to happen. "Whom shall I persuade
this time to lead back into your love? Who, Sappho,
wrongs you?
For if she runs now, soon she will chase;
if she refuses gifts, she will give them instead;
if she does not love, soon she will love,
even against her will."
Come to me now too, and free me from
harsh cares, and all that my heart
longs to have done, accomplish it; and you yourself
be my ally in the fight.
translator_note: The manuscript tradition of Dionysius is genuinely uncertain at several points, but none change the overall sense much. I follow the Perseus/Radermacher text used here: "ὄττι δἦν τὸ πέπονθα" (line 14, "what I had suffered [this] time") rather than the variant "δηὖτε πέπονθα" found in Wharton/Cox (which would mean "suffered again" instead, echoing the "again" of the next line) — the difference is minor. I also render "πείθω" (line 17) as the verb "I persuade" (the goddess/Sappho asking whom she must win over) rather than treating it as the proper name of the goddess Peitho ("Persuasion"), following the majority/Perseus reading rather than Wharton's older capitalized "Πείθω." The whole final speech of Aphrodite (lines 17-23) is rendered in quotation marks for clarity, since Greek marks it only by sense, not punctuation.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Individual phrases ("child of Zeus, weaver of wiles", "black earth", "blessed one") converge with many published versions as any literal rendering would, but the wording does not track any specific translator I recognize — not Carson ("spangled mind", "whipping their wings down the sky"), not Lattimore, Barnard, Campbell (Loeb), or Wharton's prose. Reads as freshly composed.

full_text:
Come to me here from Crete, to this holy temple,
where there is a lovely grove
of apple trees, and altars smoking
with frankincense;

and in it cold water babbles through the branches
of apple trees, and the whole place is shadowed
with roses, and from the quivering leaves
a drowsy sleep comes streaming down;

and in it a horse-grazing meadow has bloomed
with spring flowers, and the breezes
blow gently [...]
[...]

There then, Cypris, taking [...]
pour nectar delicately mingled
with the joys of the feast
into golden cups.
translator_note: Lines 11-12 are almost entirely lost on the ostracon (shown only as an open bracket in the source), so no words are supplied there. The final stanza's syntax is unusual: the Greek runs "there then you ... taking, Cypris ... pour" as one continuous imperative sentence (with a gap after "you"), rather than two separate clauses; I've rendered it as a single flowing command to match the ostracon's grammar, moving "into golden cups" to the end of the English sentence for readability while keeping all the same content. I followed the ostracon's own readings throughout rather than the shorter/variant wording quoted later by Hermogenes (who adds an explicit "wind" as subject and omits the rose-shade clause) or Athenaeus (who quotes the last stanza recast into a different grammatical frame, "Come, Cypris... pouring").

fable_review.resemblance_note: Shares the inevitable common vocabulary of this famous fragment (cold water, apple branches, golden cups, Cypris) but specific choices — "babbles", "quivering leaves", "drowsy sleep comes streaming down", "horse-grazing meadow has bloomed" — do not track any single published version (e.g. Campbell's Loeb has "sounds", "shimmering", "sleep comes down"); reads as freshly composed.

my brother may come home here,
and whatever his heart wishes to happen,
may all of it be fulfilled.

And as for all he did wrong before, may he undo it all,
and become a joy to those who love him
and a grief to his enemies — and may there come upon us
no further suffering, not one.

translator_note: Source verification passed: id and note matched the expected values. The papyrus (P.Oxy. 7) is heavily lacunose — roughly 80% of the running text is modern editorial restoration in brackets, and three editors (Blass 1898, Edmonds 1922, Campbell/Lobel-Page-Voigt) diverge on several key readings. I followed the Campbell/Voigt text (the modern scholarly standard, incorporating the joining scrap P.Oxy. 2289 fr. 6) rather than Blass's older restoration, since it is now the best-attested and most widely accepted reading. The most substantive divergence: Blass restores the opening address to the Nereids alone (with Aphrodite only implied via a vocative "ἄμβροτε" in line 5) and reads line 18 as "grievous darkness" (λύγρ᾽ ἐρέμνα); Campbell's text instead names Aphrodite/Cypris directly both at the poem's opening (line 1) and near its end (line 18, "σὺ δὲ Κύπρι σέμνα," "but you, holy Cypris"), framing the whole prayer as addressed jointly to Aphrodite and the Nereids. Lines 11–20 are so fragmentary that only isolated words or phrases survive; I have left these as literally as possible with [...] marking real gaps rather than inventing connective sense.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Sense parallels Campbell's Loeb prose ("grant that my brother arrive here unharmed... be a joy to his friends and a bane to his enemies") and Rayor's version, as any correct rendering must, but word choice and rhythm differ (e.g. "grief to his enemies", "no further suffering, not one", "a partner in his honor" are not Campbell's or Rayor's phrasings). No specific published translation is being echoed verbatim.

translator_note: Lines 1-8 are extremely lacunose and largely untranslatable beyond isolated words; I have marked these with [...] rather than inventing connective sense. For the crux at the end (lines 8-11), witnesses diverge: the 1914 editio princeps reads a comparative adjective (πικροτέραν, "more bitter") with indicative verbs and a plural subject ("they boasted"), implying unnamed people gloating over Doricha; the later standard text (Campbell/Voigt, followed here) reads a superlative (πικροτάταν, "most bitter") with optative verbs and a singular subject, making it a prayer that Doricha herself not be able to boast of ensnaring Charaxos again. I have followed the better-attested modern standard reading (superlative, optative, singular "she") as the more coherent and widely accepted text.

full_text:
Some say an army of horsemen, others of foot soldiers,
others of ships, is the most beautiful thing
upon the black earth; but I say it is
whatever a person loves.

And it is altogether easy to make this understood
by everyone: for she who far surpassed
all humankind in beauty, Helen, her husband
the very best of men

she left, and went sailing to Troy,
and neither of her child nor of her dear parents
did she think at all, but [Cypris] led her astray
the instant she saw [him]

— Cypris; for [the heart/mind] is easily bent, [...]
[...] lightly [...]
[...] now makes me think of Anactoria
who is not here beside me,

whose lovely walk I would rather see,
and the bright flash of her face,
than the chariots of the Lydians and men in full armor
fighting on foot.
translator_note: Verified the sourced entry: id "sappho-fr16" and note both match the expected values. I follow the modern Lobel-Page/Voigt reading (confirmed by P.Oxy. 2166(a)) over Grenfell & Hunt's 1914 conjecture: Helen sails to Troy of her own accord, forgetting husband and kin, and it is Cypris (Aphrodite) who leads her astray on catching sight of Paris — not the earlier guess that Helen "lost all reverence for Troy." Likewise I follow the modern "πεσδομάχεντας" (fighting on foot) rather than Grenfell & Hunt's "fighting on horseback," an opposite-sense restoration. In lines 11-12 the object seen ("him," i.e. Paris) and the subject of "for [the heart] is easily bent" are supplied for readability where the papyrus is broken; the heavily lacunose Kypris stanza (13-16) is left with [...] marking real gaps rather than invented content.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Phrasing is in the common register shared by many modern versions (Campbell, Rayor, Barnard all open similarly by necessity of the Greek), but it does not track any single published translation in distinctive word choice or rhythm — e.g. it lacks Carson's "some men say..." anaphora and Rayor's exact wording. Convergence only.

Near, now, to [the servants of the Muses] let [...] breathe,
queenly Hera, your favor, and for the festival
— the vowed one — which the sons of Atreus held
for you, kings that they were,
having accomplished it through great ordeals,
first around Ilion, and afterward,
setting out for here; for to find the way
they were unable,
until they went to you and to Zeus, god of suppliants,
and Thyone's lovely child.
But now we [...] do,
just as in the old days —
holy, and [...] the crowd
of girls [...] of women,
round about [...]
the measures of the ritual cry [...]
all [...]
[...]
to be [...]
for Hera to come [...]
translator_note: Translated from the post-2014 papyrus-based text (Ferrari's edition, combining P.GC. inv. 105 with P.Oxy. 1231/PSI 123), not the older wholly-conjectural Lobel-Page reconstruction, since the source flags that text as based on real papyrus letters rather than guesswork. Line 3's Ἀτρ[εΐδα]ι is genuinely ambiguous between nominative plural "the sons of Atreus" and dative singular "for the son of Atreus" (Menelaus alone); I followed the plural, which the source notes as one of two live possibilities. Line 9's ἀντίαον (an epithet of Zeus, roughly "of meeting/who hears suppliants") I rendered loosely as "god of suppliants" for readability. Many lines from 13 onward are too fragmentary in the papyrus to yield connected sense; I have kept the English as literal and gap-marked as the Greek rather than smoothing it into invented continuity.</translator_note>

fable_review.resemblance_note: No distinctive verbal match to any specific published translation (Rayor-Lardinois, West, Obbink, Carson); word choices like "queenly Hera," "the vowed one," "kings that they were," and "the measures of the ritual cry" diverge from the standard published renderings.

full_text:
He seems to me equal to the gods,
that man, whoever he is, who sits
across from you and, close beside you,
listens to you speaking sweetly

and laughing a laugh that stirs desire — which, I swear,
sets the heart in my chest to fluttering.
For the moment I glance at you, even briefly,
no voice comes to me anymore,

but my tongue is broken to silence, and at once
a thin fire has run beneath my skin,
my eyes see nothing at all, and my ears
are filled with a roaring.

Sweat pours down over me, and trembling
seizes me all over — I am greener than grass,
and I seem to myself to be little short
of dying.

But everything must be endured/risked, since...
translator_note: The final line is where the manuscript tradition breaks down most severely (see witness apparatus) — recensions diverge sharply on wording and the poem trails off in a lacuna. I follow the plain, best-attested manuscript-adjacent reading (ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον, ἐπεὶ...) rather than Edmonds's idiosyncratic imperative rewriting, and preserve the cutoff rather than inventing a completion. Also, at 3.1-2 ('ὡς γὰρ εἰσίδω βροχέως σε') I follow the Lobel-Page/Campbell reading (shared by two independent recensions) over Edmonds's isolated conjecture that turns 'βροχέως' into a vocative pet-name — that reading is idiosyncratic and unsupported by the manuscripts even in Edmonds's own apparatus.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Only generic convergence on unavoidable renderings ('equal to the gods', 'greener than grass'); no specific published translation matched in diction or rhythm.

note: Simile of stars around the moon, transmitted via Eustathius; often discussed alongside fr. 96.

full_text:
The stars around the beautiful moon
at once hide their shining form,
whenever, full, she shines on the earth the most.
translator_note: I translated only the three verses directly quoted by Eustathius (the sole actual verse witness), not the composite text found in later editions (e.g. Wharton's), which splices in the word ἀργυρία ("silver") from Julian's separate, non-verbatim paraphrase into a conjectural gap after γᾶν. That addition is an editorial reconstruction, not transmitted verse, so I left it out rather than inventing a line to fill it.

full_text:
Cyprus [...]...
a herald came [...] swift [...]
Idaos [...] a swift messenger,
and of the rest of Asia [...] imperishable fame:

'Hector and his companions are bringing the glancing-eyed girl
from holy Thebe and ever-flowing Placia,
delicate Andromache, on ships over the salt
sea; and many golden bracelets and garments
of purple, fragrant with perfume, dappled ornaments,
and countless silver cups and ivory.'

So he spoke; and quickly the dear father sprang up,
and word went out through the wide city to his kin.
At once the sons of Ilion, under well-wheeled carriages,
drove mules yoked, and a whole crowd of women
climbed aboard, and with them slim-ankled maidens;
and apart from them the daughters of Priam.
And men yoked horses under the chariots,
[...] young unmarried men, greatly [...]
[...] charioteers [...]
[...]

like to the gods [...]
[...] holy, all together [...]
they set out [...] toward Ilion,
and the sweet-toned pipe mingled with the lyre,
and the clatter of castanets; and clear-voiced the girls
sang a holy song, and it reached up into the sky,
a wondrous echo [...] laughing [...]
and everywhere along the roads there was
mixing-bowls and cups [...]
myrrh and cassia and frankincense mingled together;
and the older women raised the ritual cry,
and all the men cried out a lovely high song,
calling on Paon, the far-shooter, the fine-lyred one,
and they sang a hymn to Hector and Andromache, godlike.
translator_note: At the line corresponding to "the older women..." (composite line 31), the modern critical vulgate prints ἐλέλυσδον (a ritual cry-verb related to ἐλελεῦ), which I follow here as "raised the ritual cry." The raw papyrus witnesses (both P.Oxy. 1232 and 2076, per the sourced apparatus) instead show letters pointing to a form of ὀλολύζω ("ululated"), essentially the same ritual wedding/cult cry in different guise — the sense (a ceremonial female cry of celebration) is not substantially different either way.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Some phrases coincide with Campbell's Loeb ("holy Thebe and ever-flowing Placia," "delicate Andromache," "over the salt sea"), but these are near-inevitable literal renderings; word choice diverges elsewhere (e.g. "glancing-eyed," "dappled ornaments," "raised the ritual cry"), so no specific published translation appears recalled.

note: Simile comparing the onset of Eros to a wind striking mountain oaks.

lines.greek: Ἐκβακχεύεται ἐπὶ Φαίδρῳ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἔρωτος, τῇ δὲ ὁ ἔρως

shook her heart,

lines.english: as a wind falling on oaks along a mountain.

full_text:
He is driven to Bacchic frenzy over Phaedrus by love — and for her, Eros
shook her heart,
as a wind falling on oaks along a mountain.
translator_note: This fragment survives only embedded in a sentence of Maximus of Tyre (Or. 18.9), who is comparing Socrates' passion for Phaedrus to Sappho's for a girl of hers; the first line as transmitted is Maximus's own framing (about Socrates/Phaedrus), while "τῇ δὲ ὁ ἔρως ἐτίναξεν τὰς φρένας, ὡς ἄνεμος κατ᾿ ὄρος δρυσὶν ἐμπεσών" ("and for her Eros shook her heart, as a wind falling on oaks along a mountain") is the part usually taken to preserve the sense of Sappho's own image. No independent papyrus or second quotation exists. I've translated Maximus's own manuscript wording (third person, prose participle ἐμπεσών, reading κατ᾿ ὄρος) rather than later editors' conjectural first-person verse restorations (e.g. Bergk's "Eros again shook my heart..." or Voigt/Campbell's Aeolic ἐμπέτων), since that manuscript text is the actually-attested reading; the restorations shift grammatical person and diction but not the core image, a wind striking mountain oaks as a figure for love's onset.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The clause "shook her/my heart ... like/as a wind falling on oaks on a mountain" is close in wording to Campbell's Loeb rendering ("Love shook my heart like a wind falling on oaks on a mountain"), but for so short and simple a simile any literal rendering of ἐτίναξεν φρένας / ἄνεμος δρυσὶν ἐμπεσών converges on this phrasing; the third-person, Maximus-framing choices here are distinctive and not from any published version I recognize.

note: Fragment on a lover's arrival and the quieting of longing.

lines.greek: ὂν δ᾽ ἔψυξας ἔμαν φρένα καιομέναν πόθωι.
lines.english: and you cooled my heart that was burning with desire.

full_text:
You came, and [...] you did — and I was longing for you,
and you cooled my heart that was burning with desire.
translator_note: The word after ἦλθες ("you came") is corrupt in the sole manuscript witness (marked with obeli/daggers in the sourced text); editions disagree on whether to print καί, καλ', or omit it. I've rendered the line preserving that gap rather than guessing the missing sense, since no reading is clearly authoritative. ἐμαιόμαν ("I was seeking/yearning for") and ἔψυξας ("you cooled/chilled") are themselves editorial restorations of a badly damaged clause (per the apparatus), but are the best-attested readings across witnesses, so I translated them as given.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The sense inevitably converges with standard versions (e.g. Campbell's Loeb: "you have cooled my heart which was burning with desire"), but wording/word order differ enough ("that was burning" vs "which was burning", the bracketed gap treatment is distinctive) that this reads as freshly composed, not recalled.

note: Two-line couplet recalling a past love for a girl named Atthis.

lines.greek: ἠράμαν μὲν ἔγω σέθεν Ἂτθι πάλαι πότα·
lines.english: Atthis, I was in love with you once, long ago —

lines.greek: σμίκρα μοι παίς ἔμμεν᾿ ἐφαίνεο κἄχαρις.
lines.english: to me you seemed a tiny child, with no charm in you at all.

full_text:
Atthis, I was in love with you once, long ago —
to me you seemed a tiny child, with no charm in you at all.
translator_note: The two lines are a modern editorial join (Lobel): line 1 is transmitted only by Hephaestion (as a bare metrical example), line 2 only by Plutarch (in a discussion of erotic charis between women). No ancient source attests them as a single couplet, though the pairing is standard in modern editions (Lobel-Page, Voigt, Campbell). Revised from the prior draft to move away from wording that tracked Campbell's Loeb too closely: μέν is left untranslated (its answering δέ clause is lost), πάλαι πότα is rendered with the doubled temporal sense "once, long ago," σμίκρα is now "tiny" rather than "small," and κἄχαρις (= καὶ ἄχαρις, "and without charm/grace") is unpacked as a separate clause, "with no charm in you at all," rather than a compound adjective, to vary both diction and syntax from the earlier version.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The rendering is very close to D. A. Campbell's Loeb (Greek Lyric I, 1982): "I loved you, Atthis, once long ago... you seemed to me a small, graceless child." The word choices "small" + "graceless child" and the overall order track Campbell nearly verbatim; however, the fragment is so short and simple that convergence is partly expected — the match is real but the line offers few alternatives.

note: Polemic addressed to an uncultivated woman, warning of oblivion after death; transmitted by Stobaeus.

lines.greek: κατθάνοισα δὲ κείσῃ οὐδέ ποτα μναμοσύνα σέθεν
lines.english: But when you have died you will lie there, and no memory of you

full_text:
But when you have died you will lie there, and no memory of you
will ever exist, not even afterward — for you have no share of the roses
that come from Pieria; but unseen, even in the house of Hades,
you will drift among the shadowy dead, flown out from among them.
translator_note: Followed the fullest witness (Stobaeus, as printed by Voigt) rather than the shorter Plutarch quotations or Cox's conjectural rewriting of the corrupt "ποκ'/πόθα... ὔστερον" clause; that word is textually uncertain (obelized by editors) but the general sense "not even afterward/ever again" is not in serious doubt. Rendered ἐκπεποταμένα ("having flown/fluttered out/away") as "flown out from among them," capturing the image of a soul that has fluttered off into invisibility among the dim dead.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Does not match Campbell's Loeb ("flown from our midst... among the shadowy corpses"), Barnard, Carson, or other standard versions in wording or rhythm; overlaps only in sense-forced phrases like "house of Hades."

full_text:
You, girls, [busy yourselves] with the lovely gifts of the violet-robed Muses,
and with the song-loving, clear-voiced tortoiseshell lyre —
but my skin, once soft, old age now
has seized, and my hair has turned white instead of black.
My heart has grown heavy, my knees do not carry me
that were once nimble in the dance, like little fawns.
I groan over this often — but what can I do?
A human being cannot escape growing old.
For indeed they say that rose-armed Dawn once,
seized by love, went and carried Tithonos to the ends of the earth,
beautiful and young as he was — but even him, in time, grey old age
caught, though he had an immortal wife.

[...] considers [...]
[...] might grant [...]
But I love delicate refinement — [...] and this, for me,
the brightness and beauty and desire of the sun has fallen to my lot.
translator_note: Translated from TEXT A (Digital Sappho / Dickinson College Commentaries reading). Where sources diverge substantively: line 4 follows ἐπέλλαβε "seized" (vs. Wikipedia's κατέσκεθε "held fast/gripped," similar sense); line 10 follows the "seized/smitten by love" (πάσχω-type) reading over the rival "having learned love" (δα-/δαῆναι) reading, since the exact papyrus letters are damaged and disputed. Lines 1-2's opening verb is only a scrap in the papyrus (three incompatible scholarly supplements exist); I render the sense common to the "busy yourselves with/pursue" family of restorations rather than committing to one editor's exact Greek supplement. Lines 13-14 are too fragmentary (isolated verb-forms only) to translate beyond their bare gapped sense. The final couplet (here lines 15-16) is preserved whole only via Athenaeus's separate quotation, used to patch the otherwise-damaged papyrus (P.Oxy. 1787); its last word/clause is elliptical in Greek ("has obtained/fallen to my lot"), so I supply "for me" implicitly rather than inventing an explicit object beyond what the source gives.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Sense-level convergence with standard versions (West 2005, Rayor) is inevitable for this well-known poem, but wording differs from those I can recall (e.g. West's 'You for the fragrant-bosomed Muses' lovely gifts / be zealous, girls'). No specific match in diction, order, or rhythm to a published translation.

sweet god — truly you [...] terrible griefs for me

translator_note: The papyrus itself preserves only the address to "Dream" (ὄνοιρε/Ὄνειρε) and, per line 3, a "sweet god" bringing "terrible griefs" — no vocative to Aphrodite or explicit mention of night survives in the actual letters; those associations come from editorial conjecture about the poem's context (per the sourced witness notes), not from extant text, so I have not invented them in translation. I followed the Voigt/Campbell standard text (ὄνοιρε, the papyrus's own -οι- spelling) rather than Grenfell & Hunt's 1922 normalized "Ὄνειρε," since that is the modern critical consensus reading; the difference is orthographic, not semantic. Line 4's ζά is the Aeolic/Lesbian form of διά ("through/greatly"), rendered here as "apart." All bracketed gaps in the Greek are left unfilled in English, per the source's own caution that the surrounding conjectural supplements (e.g. "black wings," "black night") are the 1922 editors' proposals, not part of the transmitted text.

full_text:
I wish, truly, that I were dead.
She left me, weeping bitterly,
and said this to me, among many things:
"Ah, what terrible things we have suffered —
Sappho, I swear I leave you against my will."

And I answered her this:
"Go, and be happy, and remember me —
for you know how we cherished you.

But if not, then I want
to remind you [...]
[...] and the lovely things we knew together —

for with many garlands of violets
and of roses and of crocuses together
[...] you crowned yourself, beside me,

and many woven wreaths
of flowers, made with your own hands,
you set around your soft neck,

and with much perfume,
the fragrant oil of bregthos [...]
you anointed yourself, and with royal myrrh too,

and on a soft couch,
tender, [...]
you let out your longing for [...] the girls,

and there was no [...] nor any
shrine, nor [...]
place from which we two were absent,

no grove [...] dance
[...] sound
[...] song
translator_note: Translated primarily from Recension A (Campbell/Loeb text), the standard modern reading of this unique Berlin parchment witness. Bracketed gaps are preserved as [...] rather than filled, per instructions, even where Recension B offers editorial supplements (e.g. line 11's ὄσ[σα μόλθακα], line 23's αἶψα νεα[νίδων]) — those conjectures are plausible but not certain enough to present as translated text. "βρένθειον" (line 19) is left as a transliterated descriptor ("bregthos") since it names a specific, not fully identified type of perfume/unguent rather than a common noun with an established English equivalent. The dramatic situation (a friend or beloved departing, recalling shared garlands, perfumes, and choral dancing) is clear despite the fragmentary final stanzas.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Phrasing overlaps only in ways any competent literal rendering converges on (e.g. "I leave you against my will," "soft neck"). It does not match the distinctive wording of Campbell's Loeb prose, Barnard, Carson ("I simply want to be dead"), or Rayor in word choice or rhythm.

lines.greek: κῆθι δ' ἔλθην ἀμμ . [ . .] . .ισα τό̣δ' οὐ
lines.english: and to go there [...] this not
[...] much
[...] sounds [...] between.

lines.greek: ε]ὔ̣μαρ[ες μ]ὲ̣ν οὐκ̣ ἄμ̣μι θέαισι μόρ-
lines.english: It is not easy for us to match
the lovely form of goddesses
[...] you have [...]
and [...] Aphrodite
[...] poured nectar from
a golden [...]
[...] with her hands, Persuasion [...]
[...] the Geraistion
[...] dear friends

full_text:
[...] Sardis [...]
often turning her mind here,
as [...] we [...] [...]
you, like a goddess plain to see
and known to all — and in your singing she delighted most.
But now she stands out among the Lydian
women, as when the sun
has set, the rose-fingered moon
outshines all the stars; and its light
stretches over the salt sea
equally, and over the flower-thick fields;
and the lovely dew is poured down, and roses
bloom, and tender
chervil, and melilot rich in flower.
And often, pacing back and forth, remembering
gentle Atthis with longing,
her delicate heart is eaten away with grief, somehow;
and to go there [...] this not
[...] much
[...] sounds [...] between.
It is not easy for us to match
the lovely form of goddesses
[...] you have [...]
[...]
[...]
and [...] Aphrodite
[...] poured nectar from
a golden [...]
[...] with her hands, Persuasion [...]
[...]
[...]
[...]
[...] the Geraistion
[...] dear friends
[...] no one [...]
[...] will come [...]
translator_note: Followed the Campbell/Lobel/Voigt main text (aoidoi.org / Digital Sappho) rather than West's conjectural ὡς ὅτ' at line 7 or Edmonds' largely conjectural 1922 recension, since the Voigt-based text is the majority modern reading and closer to what survives on the papyrus. Line "λέπταν ποι φρένα κ[ᾶ]ρ[ι σᾷ] βόρηται" follows Campbell's restoration (heart eaten away by grief); Lobel/Moore's alternative "κῆρ δ' ἄσᾳ" gives a similar sense (heart consumed with anguish), so the translation would not change much either way. From roughly line 18 onward the papyrus is too damaged for connected sense; isolated legible words (Aphrodite, nectar, golden, Persuasion, the Geraistion, dear [friends]) are rendered where they appear, with gaps left as [...] rather than invented.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Shares inevitable phrases with standard versions ("rose-fingered moon," "outshines all the stars") but distinctive choices ("flower-thick fields," "pacing back and forth," "melilot rich in flower") do not match any specific published translation.

note: Paired fragments on hairbands/headdresses across three generations of women (Sappho's mother, Sappho, her daughter Cleis), set against a backdrop of political exile.

lines.english: ...for she who gave birth to me
used to say that in her own youth a great
adornment it was, if a girl wore in her hair
a band wound round with purple,
that this indeed was so —
but a girl whose hair was more golden than
a blazing torch could better wear
garlands fitted close
of richly blooming flowers;
and just now a headband...
an embroidered one, from Sardis
...the Ionian cities...
But for you, Cleis, an embroidered
headband — I have no way to get one,
none at all; but to the man of Mytilene
if [...] embroidered [...]
these things, of the Cleanactidae's
exile — [the text here is corrupt] —
are reminders; for terribly did [everything] drain away

full_text:
...for she who gave birth to me
used to say that in her own youth a great
adornment it was, if a girl wore in her hair
a band wound round with purple,
that this indeed was so —
but a girl whose hair was more golden than
a blazing torch could better wear
garlands fitted close
of richly blooming flowers;
and just now a headband...
an embroidered one, from Sardis
...the Ionian cities...

But for you, Cleis, an embroidered
headband — I have no way to get one,
none at all; but to the man of Mytilene
[...] to have [...]
if [...] embroidered [...]
these things, of the Cleanactidae's
exile — [the text here is corrupt] —
are reminders; for terribly did [everything] drain away
translator_note: Source verified: id and note match. 98a is a mother-speaks-of-her-youth passage recalling that a purple hairband was once the height of fashion, though the speaker suggests golden-haired girls suit flower garlands even better; a Sardis-made headband is then mentioned. 98b turns to Sappho's own daughter Cleis, for whom she cannot obtain a fine embroidered headband, explaining that such luxuries are now bound up with the political exile of the Cleanactidae clan (a Mytilenean faction) — the source's line 12 has a minor editorial disagreement (πόλ{ε}ις vs πόλις, spelling only) and 98b line 8 contains an obelized crux left untranslated as corrupt, per the source's own apparatus. Heavy lacunae throughout both fragments are preserved with [...] rather than invented.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Differs from Campbell (Loeb), Rayor, and Carson in diction and word order; shared vocabulary (purple band, Sardis, headband) is inevitable convergence for this Greek.

note: Short dialogue-style complaint to her mother about being unable to weave, overcome by desire for a boy through Aphrodite's agency.

lines.greek: γλύκηα μᾶτερ, οὔτοι δύναμαι κρέκην τὸν ἴστον
lines.english: Sweet mother, I cannot work the loom,

lines.greek: πόθῳ δάμεισα παῖδος βραδίναν δι' Ἀφροδίταν
lines.english: overcome with longing for a boy, by slender Aphrodite's power.

full_text:
Sweet mother, I cannot work the loom,
overcome with longing for a boy, by slender Aphrodite's power.
translator_note: βραδίναν ("slender/soft") could modify either the boy (παῖδος) or Aphrodite (δι' Ἀφροδίταν) since it's adjacent to the latter but could agree with either in gender/case; many editors take it to describe the boy's slender/graceful form, with Aphrodite as the agent of the desire, but the syntax is genuinely ambiguous given the word order. I rendered it attached to Aphrodite as printed word order suggests, but "longing for a slender boy" is an equally defensible reading.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Opening "Sweet mother, I cannot..." is forced by the Greek; the rest diverges from Campbell ("ply the loom... slender Aphrodite") and other standard versions in wording and rhythm.

note: Address to Hesperus, the evening star.

lines.greek: Ἔσπερε πάντα φέρων ὅσα φαίνολις ἐσκέδασ᾽ Αὔως.
lines.english: Evening Star, bringing back everything that shining Dawn scattered,

lines.greek: Ἕσπερε, πάντα φέρεις, φέρεις ὄϊν, φέρεις αἶγα, φέρεις ματέρι παῖδα.
lines.english: Evening Star, you bring everything back — you bring the sheep, you bring the goat, you bring the child home to its mother.

full_text:
Evening Star, bringing back everything that shining Dawn scattered,
Evening Star, you bring everything back — you bring the sheep, you bring the goat, you bring the child home to its mother.
translator_note: These two lines are not quoted together by any single ancient source: Demetrius (On Style §141) quotes only the second line, to illustrate anaphora of φέρεις ("you bring"), while the Etymologicum Magnum quotes only the first, to gloss the Aeolic word for "dawn." Modern editions conventionally print them as one two-line fragment, a conflation followed here. The two witnesses also disagree on the verb form of the address itself — participle φέρων ("bringing") in the Etymologicum Magnum vs. finite φέρεις ("you bring") in Demetrius — reflecting that each source preserves a different syntactic continuation; I kept each witness's own verb in its own line rather than harmonizing them. I did not adopt the disputed, non-attested insertion of ἄπυ ("away/home") before "mother" found in some modern composite editions (Wharton, Edmonds), since it is an editorial supplement, not a reading in either primary witness — though I let "home" stand in the English of that line as a natural rendering of an implied return, not a translation of that disputed word.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The wording overlaps in sense with many published versions (e.g. the common "Evening Star, you bring all that the shining dawn scattered") but the specific phrasing here — the em-dash construction, "shining Dawn", "you bring the sheep, you bring the goat" — does not match any single translator's diction/rhythm (Barnard, Carson, Lombardo, Rayor, Campbell) closely enough to indicate recall rather than convergence on a very short, simple text.

id: Sappho fr. 105a (Voigt/Lobel-Page numbering) — "the sweet apple on the topmost bough"
note: Simile of an unreachable apple ripening on the highest bough, cited by ancient critics as bridal imagery.

lines.greek: οἶον τὸ γλυκύμαλον ἐρεύθεται ἄκρωι ἐπ᾽ ὔσδωι,
lines.english: As the sweet apple reddens on the topmost branch,

lines.greek: ἄκρον ἐπ᾽ ἀκροτάτωι, λελάθοντο δὲ μαλοδρόπηες·
lines.english: at the top of the topmost bough — and the apple-pickers forgot it,

lines.greek: οὐ μὰν ἐκλελάθοντ᾽, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐδύναντ᾽ ἐπίκεσθαι.
lines.english: no, not quite forgot it, but they could not reach it.

full_text:
As the sweet apple reddens on the topmost branch,
at the top of the topmost bough — and the apple-pickers forgot it,
no, not quite forgot it, but they could not reach it.
translator_note: Text follows the sole verbatim ancient witness (the Scholiast on Hermogenes = Syrianus), where all consulted digitizations agree on wording and word order; only accentuation/punctuation differ between copies, none affecting meaning. λελάθοντο (line 2) is rendered "forgot," picked up and qualified by οὐκ ἐκλελάθοντ᾽ ("not quite forgot") in line 3, preserving the original's turn from apparent neglect to simple inability to reach the fruit — the poem's core image of an unattainable, ripening bride.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Sense overlaps with famous versions (e.g. Anne Carson's "no, not forgot: were unable to reach"), but word choice and rhythm differ enough that this reads as freshly composed, not recalled from a specific edition.

id: Sappho fr. 105(c) Lobel-Page / 105c Voigt (= Bergk, PLG⁴, Sappho fr. 94; = Edmonds, Lyra Graeca i, Sappho frr. 151–152) — the hyacinth simile
note: Simile of a hyacinth trampled underfoot by shepherds in the mountains; also numbered 105(c) in Lobel-Page.

lines.greek: οἵαν τὰν ὑάκινθον ἐν οὔρεσι ποιμένες ἄνδρες
lines.english: Like the hyacinth that shepherd men, up in the mountains,
trample down underfoot,
and on the ground lies the purple flower —

full_text:
Like the hyacinth that shepherd men, up in the mountains,
trample down underfoot,
and on the ground lies the purple flower —
translator_note: The sole witness (Demetrius, On Style §106, via ms. P) transmits the second colon as a verbless nominal clause, χαμαὶ δέ τε πορφύρον ἄνθος, "and on the ground [is] the purple flower," which I follow here. Bergk's widely-reprinted emendation χάμαι δ᾽ ἐπιπορφύρει ἄνθος supplies a finite verb, giving "and the flower turns/glows purple on the ground" — a livelier but conjectural reading (Roberts notes a metrical objection to it). I chose the unemended manuscript text as the better-attested reading, per the task's instruction to prefer the best-attested version.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Wording overlaps with standard versions (e.g. "the purple flower", "trample underfoot") only in the way any literal rendering of this short simile must; it does not reproduce the distinctive phrasing of Wharton's literal version, Edmonds' Loeb, Barnard, or Carson ("like the hyacinth in the mountains that shepherd men / with their feet trample down") in word order or rhythm.

note: Wedding hymn calling on carpenters to raise the roof-beam, comparing the bridegroom to Ares.

lines.english: Raise the roof-beam high—
lift it, carpenter men!
Hymenaeus!
The bridegroom is coming, the equal of Ares,
far greater than a big man,

lines.greek: πέρροχος ὡς ὄτ᾽ ἀοιδὸς ὁ Λέσβιος ἀλλοδαποῖσιν.
lines.english: as far surpassing as the Lesbian singer surpasses men of other lands.

full_text:
Raise the roof-beam high—
lift it, carpenter men!
Hymenaeus!
The bridegroom is coming, the equal of Ares,
far greater than a big man,
as far surpassing as the Lesbian singer surpasses men of other lands.
translator_note: This fragment survives only as two separate ancient quotations (Hephaestion and Demetrius) that disagree on wording at several points and were joined into one poem only by modern editors. I followed Hephaestion for the opening roof-beam lines and the refrain (ἔρχεται "comes," not Demetrius's εἰσέρχεται "enters"), and added Demetrius's two further lines (the "greater than a big man" line and the πέρροχος/"Lesbian singer" couplet), which are not linked to the roof-beam lines in any ancient source but are conventionally printed together as Voigt/Lobel-Page fr. 111.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The famous phrasing here is Wharton/Salinger's "Raise high the roof beam, carpenters"; this version's "Raise the roof-beam high— / lift it, carpenter men!" deliberately differs in word order and diction. Phrases like "the equal of Ares" overlap with Campbell's Loeb ("like Ares") only at the level any literal rendering would; no specific published translation is matched in wording or rhythm.

note: Wedding hymn praising the bridegroom's good fortune and the bride's grace.

lines.greek: ὄλβιε γαμβρέ, σοὶ μὲν δὴ γάμος, ὡς ἄραο,
lines.english: Happy bridegroom, now your marriage,

lines.greek: ἐκτετέλεστ᾽, ἔχῃς δὲ παρθένον, ἂν ἄραο.
lines.english: just as you prayed, is accomplished, and you have the maiden you prayed for.

lines.greek: μελλίχροος δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἱμερτῷ κέχυται προσώπῳ.
lines.english: and a honeyed grace is poured over her lovely face.

full_text:
Happy bridegroom, now your marriage,
just as you prayed, is accomplished, and you have the maiden you prayed for.
and a honeyed grace is poured over her lovely face.
translator_note: The third line's implied subject (something like "charm" or "sweetness," feminine, agreeing with μελλίχροος) is not stated in the surviving Greek, so "grace" is supplied as the natural sense rather than a literal word. Manuscripts vary between ἔχῃς/ἔχεις ("you have/may you have") — translated here as a simple present fact ("you have") following the C/P reading rather than ms. I's ἔχεις, though the difference in meaning is minor.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Converges in sense with Wharton's and Campbell's renderings (inevitable for a short, simple couplet) but not in specific wording.

note: Dialogue between the bride and personified Virginity at the moment of its departure.

lines.greek: Παρθενία, παρθενία, ποῖ με λίποισ᾽ ἀποίχῃ;
lines.english: Virginity, virginity, where have you gone, leaving me behind?

lines.greek: Οὐκέτι ἥξω πρὸς σέ, οὐκέτι ἥξω.
lines.english: Never again will I come to you, never again will I come.

full_text:
Virginity, virginity, where have you gone, leaving me behind?
Never again will I come to you, never again will I come.
translator_note: Two textual forms exist: the manuscript's own reading (λιποῦσα οἴχῃ, Koine-style) and the Aeolic-restored vulgate (λίποισ᾽ ἀποίχῃ) used by Bergk/Wharton and standard modern editions (= Lobel-Page/Voigt fr. 114). I follow the latter, more widely printed form, translated here as a single continuous question-and-answer exchange: the bride's cry to personified Virginity, and Virginity's reply.

fable_review.resemblance_note: The second line's structure echoes Wharton's literal version ("Never again will I come to thee, never again will I come"), but this Greek is so short and formulaic that virtually all literal translations converge on this wording; word choice here ("you" not "thee", "Virginity" not "Maidenhood") differs from the versions I recognize, so no specific memorization is indicated.

note: Definition of Eros as bittersweet and limb-loosening; address to Atthis.

lines.greek: Ἔρος δαῦτέ μ᾽ ὁ λυσιμελὴς δόνει,
lines.english: Once again limb-loosening Eros shakes me,
a sweet-bitter creeping thing there's no fighting off—

lines.greek: Ἄτθι, σοὶ δ᾽ ἔμεθεν μὲν ἀπήχθετο
lines.english: Atthis, thinking of me has grown hateful to you,
and you fly off after Andromeda.

full_text:
Once again limb-loosening Eros shakes me,
a sweet-bitter creeping thing there's no fighting off—
Atthis, thinking of me has grown hateful to you,
and you fly off after Andromeda.
translator_note: These are two separately transmitted couplets (Voigt/L-P frr. 130 and 131), quoted together by Hephaestion as one metrical example; I translate them as given. Line 4 follows Bentley's conjectural φροντίσδην ("to think of/care for"), the reading needed for sense against the manuscripts' corrupt φροντίς δ᾽ ἦν; πότη is taken as "flies/flits" (Aeolic for πέτομαι), i.e. Atthis's attention has turned to someone named Andromeda. Revised line 2 to render γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον more literally as a compound "sweet-bitter" adjective plus "creeping thing," and ἀμάχανον as "there's no fighting off" (lit. "against which one is powerless/without resource"), moving away from a prior phrasing ("bittersweet, irresistible creature") that echoed a published translation's word choice and order too closely.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Line 2 "that bittersweet, irresistible creature" closely echoes D. A. Campbell's Loeb (Greek Lyric I): "the bitter-sweet, irresistible creature" — same three-word choice and order (irresistible + creature for ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον is a distinctive pairing, not forced by the Greek). The rest of the translation diverges from Campbell (he has "makes me tremble" not "shakes me"), so the resemblance is one recalled phrase rather than a wholesale copy.

id: Sappho fr. 132 (Voigt / Lobel-Page numbering; "on Cleis, likened to a golden flower")
note: Short poem on her daughter Cleis, likened to a golden flower.

lines.greek: Ἔστι μοι κάλα πάϊς, χρυσίοισιν ἀνθέμοισιν
lines.english: I have a beautiful child, whose form is like
golden flowers — Cleis, my beloved,

lines.greek: ἀντί τᾶς ἔγω οὐδὲ Λυδίαν παῖσαν οὐδ' ἔρανναν.
lines.english: for whom I would not take all Lydia, nor lovely [Lydia].

full_text:
I have a beautiful child, whose form is like
golden flowers — Cleis, my beloved,
for whom I would not take all Lydia, nor lovely [Lydia].
translator_note: Line 3 has no expressed verb of exchange ("would not take" is supplied to render the elliptical ἀντί τᾶς construction, standard for this fragment). The final word ἔρανναν ("lovely") lacks a noun to modify in the surviving text; most editors take it as agreeing with an implied repetition of Λυδίαν, rendered here as "[Lydia]" in brackets to mark that supplement.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Line 3 "for whom I would not take all Lydia" is close in shape to D. A. Campbell's Loeb ("for whom I would not (take) all Lydia or lovely..."), but this is the standard elliptical rendering of ἀντί τᾶς ... οὐδὲ Λυδίαν παῖσαν that nearly all translators converge on; the rest of the translation ("whose form is like golden flowers", "my beloved" vs Campbell's "looks like golden flowers", "darling Cleis") diverges in word choice, so no specific-copy match.

note: The 'moon has set' / Midnight-poem quatrain; preserved without attribution in Hephaestion's metrical handbook, so Sapphic authorship is disputed among editors (= Page, PMG adesp. 976); included in Voigt's corpus.

lines.english: The moon has set,
and the Pleiades; it is the middle
of the night, the hour goes by,
and I lie alone.

full_text:
The moon has set,
and the Pleiades; it is the middle
of the night, the hour goes by,
and I lie alone.
translator_note: Line 4: κατεύδω/καθεύδω both mean "sleep," so "I lie alone" leans slightly interpretive for rhythm/tone — a more literal rendering would be "I sleep alone." No other substantive ambiguity affects meaning; the σελάννα/σελάνα and ἔρχετ'/ἔρχεθ' variants noted in the apparatus are spelling/dialect differences only, not differences in sense.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Phrasing overlaps with common renderings (Campbell's Loeb "The moon has set and the Pleiades; it is midnight, and time goes by, and I lie alone" is close in sense), but the specific wording "it is the middle / of the night, the hour goes by" does not match any single published translation verbatim; convergence is expected for so short and simple a text.

note: Previously unknown poem on anxiety over Charaxos' seafaring and hope for the maturation of brother Larichos; published 2014 from the Obbink papyrus; overlaps thematically with Voigt/Lobel-Page frr. 5, 9, 15-18.

lines.english: But you always chatter that Charaxos is coming,

lines.greek: νᾶϊ σὺν πλήαι. τὰ μὲν̣ οἴο̣μα̣ι Ζεῦς
lines.english: his ship full. These things, I suppose, Zeus

lines.greek: οἶδε σύμπαντές τε θέοι · σὲ δ' οὐ χρῆ
lines.english: knows, and all the gods with him; but you must not
keep thinking of these things,

lines.greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ πέμπην ἔμε καὶ κέλεσθαι
lines.english: but rather send me off, and bid me
pray many times to queen Hera
that he arrive here, bringing safely
his ship, Charaxos,

lines.greek: κἄμμ' ἐπεύρην ἀρτ̣έ̣μεας. τὰ δ' ἄλλα
lines.english: and find us unharmed. As for the rest,
let us leave it all to the gods;
for calm weather comes swiftly
out of great storms.
Those for whom the king of Olympus wishes
a guardian spirit, now, as helper out of hardship,
to turn them round, those people become blessed
and rich in good fortune.

lines.greek: κἄμμες, αἴ κε τὰν κεφάλα̣ν ἀέρρ̣η
lines.english: And we too, if he should lift his head,

lines.greek: Λάρι̣χος καὶ δή ποτ' ἄνη̣ρ γένηται,
lines.english: if Larichos should at last become a man,

lines.greek: καὶ μάλ' ἐκ πόλλαν βαρ̣υθυ̣μίαν̣ κεν
lines.english: then indeed from much heaviness of heart
we would swiftly be freed.

full_text:
But you always chatter that Charaxos is coming,
his ship full. These things, I suppose, Zeus
knows, and all the gods with him; but you must not
keep thinking of these things,
but rather send me off, and bid me
pray many times to queen Hera
that he arrive here, bringing safely
his ship, Charaxos,
and find us unharmed. As for the rest,
let us leave it all to the gods;
for calm weather comes swiftly
out of great storms.
Those for whom the king of Olympus wishes
a guardian spirit, now, as helper out of hardship,
to turn them round, those people become blessed
and rich in good fortune.
And we too, if he should lift his head,
if Larichos should at last become a man,
then indeed from much heaviness of heart
we would swiftly be freed.
translator_note: Line 17 has a substantive textual crux between witnesses: digitalsappho.org reads τὰν κεφάλαν ("the head"), while the CHS/Nagy transcription reads ϝὰν κεφάλαν ("his own head," with digamma-initial possessive). I follow the ϝὰν reading in sense ("lift his own head") since it is more idiomatic and the meaning is effectively identical either way. The addressee of the poem (traditionally taken as the speaker's mother) is implied by context but not named in the surviving lines.

fable_review.resemblance_note: Shares unavoidable convergent phrasing with published versions (e.g. "chatter" for θρύλησθα appears in several), but no sustained match in word choice, order, or rhythm with a specific published translation such as Obbink's, Rayor's, or West's.

note: Newly recovered continuation/correction of fr. 26 Voigt from the same 2014 papyrus, addressing Kypris/Aphrodite on recurring erotic suffering; substantially revises the sense of the previously known fragmentary lines.

lines.greek: πῶϲ κε δή τιϲ οὐ θαμέωϲ ἄϲαιτο,
lines.english: How could anyone not often be sickened with grief,
Kypris, mistress, over whomever she loves
and wishes, above all, to call back again?
[...] what [longing] do you hold —
[...] with what tossing seas, vainly, to tear me apart,
with a longing that unstrings the knees [...]
[...] you — I want [...]
[...] to suffer this [...]
but I, of myself,
know this well.
[too fragmentary to translate]

full_text:
How could anyone not often be sickened with grief,
Kypris, mistress, over whomever she loves
and wishes, above all, to call back again?
[...] what [longing] do you hold —
[...] with what tossing seas, vainly, to tear me apart,
with a longing that unstrings the knees [...]
[...] me not [...]
[...]
[...] you — I want [...]
[...] to suffer this [...]
but I, of myself,
know this well.
[too fragmentary to translate]
translator_note: Text follows Obbink's articulated composite (P. Sapph. Obbink corroborated by P. Oxy. 1231), lines numbered 1-13 per his Kypris-Poem internal numbering. Lines 4-9 are heavily lacunose in the papyrus and I have kept the gaps rather than guess at the missing verbs/nouns; only scattered words (e.g. "vainly," "tear apart," "knees," "you," "I want") are securely legible. Lines 11-12 (ἔγω δ' ἐμ' αὔται τοῦτο ϲύνοιδα) come only from the secondhand citation in Apollonius Dyscolus, not from either papyrus directly, per the source's caveats. ἄϲαιτο (line 1) is from a verb meaning "to be sated to the point of revulsion/distress" — rendered here as "be sickened with grief" to capture the sense of painful surfeit rather than simple sadness.</translator_note>

fable_review.resemblance_note: Phrasing ("be sickened with grief," "tossing seas," "unstrings the knees") does not match Obbink, Rayor, or West's published versions; appears freshly composed.
